2.  It is hard to miscount: no rows of zeros.
3.  The power shows the size at a glance.
Your calculator switches to it when the answer will not fit on the screen.

A number is in standard form when it is written as

$A \times 10^{n}$

where $1 \le A < 10$ and $n$ is an integer.
$1 \le 9.99 < 10$, and the power can be negative

els.text:
•  Standard form is $A \times 10^{n}$ with $1 \le A < 10$ and $n$ an integer.
•  Large: write the number as $A$ times a 1 with zeros, then as a power of ten; or peel off one ten at a time.
•  Small: write $A$, divide by a power of ten, and the power is negative.
•  Down one place, the power goes up by $1$. Up one place, the power goes down by $1$.

summary: Why we use standard form, and converting large and small numbers both ways. Large numbers: two methods (one step, or one ten at a time). Small numbers: write the first number between 1 and 10, then divide by a power of ten. The place value grid then gives the quicker rule (down a place, power up 1). Numbers in parts come last of all. Whiteboards have five questions and no hints. Printed Sheets 1 and 2 are placeholders. All questions are authored.
